claim: The rhomboid (rho) enhancer directs gene expression in the presumptive neuroectoderm under the control of the activator Dorsal, a homolog of NF-κB.
source: The rhomboid (rho) enhancer directs gene expression in the presumptive neuroectoderm under the control of the activator Dorsal, a homolog of NF-κB.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Introduction section and is supported by the experimental design described throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Twist activator and Snail repressor provide additional essential inputs to the rhomboid enhancer.
source: The Twist activator and Snail repressor provide additional essential inputs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the binding sites for these factors.

claim: 38 enhancer variants were systematically created by mutating activator and repressor binding sites in the rho neuroectodermal enhancer.
source: We systematically mutated all activator and repressor binding sites in rho neurectodermal enhancer, removing Dorsal or Twist sites individually or in pairs to diminish activation, and removing multiple Snail sites to reduce repression (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1). All 38 enhancers were cloned and integrated into the fly genome using a site-specific integration vector (Bischof et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes the systematic mutagenesis approach and references the methods used.

claim: Expression data from a total of 935 images was analyzed, with a minimum of ten embryos per construct.
source: Expression data from a total of 935 images - a minimum of ten embryos per construct - was normalized and combined to provide average expression patterns for each enhancer variant (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of images analyzed.

claim: Mutation of any single Dorsal or Twist activator binding site resulted in a measurable reduction of peak intensity and retraction of the rho stripe from the dorsal region.
source: Mutation of any single Dorsal or Twist activator binding site resulted in a measurable reduction of peak intensity and retraction of the rho stripe from the dorsal region, where activators Dorsal and Twist are present in limiting concentrations (Liberman et al., 2009; Rushlow et al., 1989).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and supported by citations to previous work on activator concentrations.

claim: Elimination of any single activator site individually reduced gene expression to approximately 60% of the peak wild-type level.
source: Strikingly, despite the differences in predicted binding affinities and relative positions of the motifs, the elimination of any site individually had similar quantitative effects, reducing gene expression to approximately 60% of the peak wild-type level (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements shown in figures and supplementary data.

claim: The impact of mutation of combinations of two Dorsal or Twist binding sites was highly variable, ranging from slightly lower expression to almost complete loss of activity.
source: In contrast to this uniform picture, the impact of mutation of combinations of two Dorsal or Twist binding sites was highly variable, ranging from slightly lower expression to almost complete loss of activity (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the variable effects observed in double mutants with supporting figures.

claim: Mutation of all four Snail sites caused pervasive expression in the mesoderm.
source: Mutation of all four Snail sites caused pervasive expression in the mesoderm, as expected, while constructs with a single intact Snail2 or Snail3 site showed substantial but not complete repression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental results of Snail site mutations.

claim: Snail1 and Snail4 motifs were not nearly as effective at mediating repression as Snail2 and Snail3, although these have similar binding affinities.
source: Snail1 and Snail4 motifs were not nearly as effective at mediating repression, although these have similar binding affinities (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript compares the effectiveness of different Snail sites despite similar binding affinities.

claim: 120 different thermodynamic models were created by combining 15 cooperativity formulations with 8 quenching formulations.
source: In all, 15 formulations for cooperativity and eight formulations for quenching were employed (Table 1). Combining these two types of formulations resulted in 120 different models, which were trained on the quantitative expression data of the 38 enhancer variants.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the model generation approach.

claim: Best overall fits were observed using a model with cooperativity values parameterized in three 'bins' of 60 bp (scheme C14) and quenching in four small 25 or 35 bp bins (schemes Q5 and Q6).
source: Best overall fits were observed using a model with cooperativity values parameterized in three 'bins' of 60 bp (scheme C14) and quenching in four small 25 or 35 bp bins (schemes Q5 and Q6).
evidence: The manuscript identifies the best-performing model structures based on RMSE analysis.

claim: Models with more parameters tended to outperform those with the fewest, but this was not a strict correlation.
source: Models with more parameters tended to outperform those with the fewest, as expected, but it was notable that this was not a strict correlation; the models with the most parameters were not as effective as those with fewer.
evidence: The manuscript analyzes the relationship between model complexity and performance.

claim: The variable effects of different pairwise mutations indicate that there are multiple and distinct thresholds for specific biochemical events occurring on the enhancer.
source: We hypothesize that the variable effects of different pairwise mutations, as opposed to the rather similar effects of individual site loss, indicates that there are multiple and distinct thresholds for specific biochemical events occurring on the enhancer.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on the observed data patterns.

claim: Parameters were estimated using CMA-ES, a global genetic algorithm.
source: Parameters were estimated using CMA-ES, a global genetic algorithm, and overall performance was calculated from the fit to all constructs, using root mean square error (RMSE) as the objective function (Hansen et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational methods used for parameter estimation.

claim: Constructs containing the wild-type ensemble of activators were among those that were less well fit than the bulk of constructs.
source: Some constructs were fit generally less well by most models. Those constructs containing the wild-type ensemble of activators (columns 1, 25, 28, 32) were among those that were less well fit than the bulk of constructs, from which we had removed activator sites
evidence: The manuscript analyzes construct-specific model performance.

claim: Three similar but non-identical PWMs were tested for each transcription factor (Dorsal, Twist, and Snail).
source: Three similar but non-identical PWMs were tested for each factor, and all possible combinations of these PWMs were utilized in refitting the data set with a selection of 24 of the entire set of models, including most of the top performers.
evidence: The manuscript describes testing different PWM combinations.

claim: Overall ranks of model performance remained similar across different PWM combinations, although RMSEs were lowest using the Snail PWM employed in the global analysis.
source: Overall ranks of model performance remained similar, although RMSEs were lowest using the PWM of Snail that was employed in the global analysis in Figure 2; this PWM predicted all four sites previously identified by in vitro footprinting (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript compares model performance across different PWM settings.

claim: The biophysical information about protein-DNA interactions for the transcription factors in this system appears to be sufficiently complete to provide a robust platform for thermodynamic modeling.
source: Thus, the biophysical information about protein-DNA interactions for the transcription factors in this system appears to be sufficiently complete to provide a robust platform for thermodynamic modeling.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the PWM testing results.

claim: Removal of entire classes of constructs had a more profound impact on model performance than removal of randomly selected constructs.
source: In general, removal of entire classes of constructs had a more profound impact than removal of randomly selected constructs.
evidence: The manuscript describes cross-validation results comparing systematic vs. random data removal.

claim: The omission of the Snail repressor site constructs resulted in striking increases in RMSE for all Snail constructs in almost all models.
source: The most profound effects were seen with the omission of the Snail repressor site constructs, where almost all models had striking increases in RMSE for all Snail constructs.
evidence: The manuscript analyzes the impact of leaving out specific construct types during cross-validation.

claim: The elimination of activator sites alone is not sufficient to provide insights into how Snail affects the enhancer's expression.
source: Evidently, the elimination of activator sites alone is not sufficient to provide insights into how Snail affects the enhancer's expression.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cross-validation analysis.

claim: Overall model performance was improved by specifying separate parameters for activator and repressor cooperativity.
source: First, overall model performance was improved by specifying separate parameters for activator and repressor cooperativity (Figure 2A; C1-9 vs. C10-C15).
evidence: The manuscript compares model performance across different cooperativity parameterization schemes.

claim: Repressor-repressor cooperativities were consistently small in models with separate parameters for activator and repressor cooperativity.
source: In these latter models, repressor-repressor cooperativities were consistently small, implying that different Snail sites did not show more than additive contributions, a finding that is consistent with the induction of localized chromatin compaction by this class of short-range repressor, which may interfere with simultaneous interactions by repressors (Li and Arnosti, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript analyzes parameter values and relates them to biological mechanisms with citation support.

claim: Activator-activator cooperativities were uniformly high and in general did not show sharp distance dependencies.
source: Activator-activator cooperativities were in contrast uniformly high, and in general did not show sharp distance dependencies.
evidence: The manuscript analyzes parameter values across models.

claim: The loose cooperative interactions of activators would explain the need for clustering of these proteins' binding sites without strong constraints on their exact positioning.
source: The loose cooperative interactions of activators would explain the need for clustering of these proteins' binding sites without strong constraints on their exact positioning, a flexibility that is seen with many developmental enhancers (Figure 4B; Arnosti and Kulkarni, 2005).
evidence: This is presented as an interpretation of the parameter values with citation support.

claim: Distance-dependence of transcriptional repression was noted in many but not all models.
source: A second trend noted in many but not all models was the distance-dependence of transcriptional repression, a feature inferred from previous studies of the Knirps, Snail, and Giant short-range repressors (Gray et al., 1994; Arnosti et al., 1996; Hewitt et al., 1999); (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript identifies this trend in parameter values and relates it to previous studies.

claim: Most parameters showed extensive mutual dependence and compensation, evidenced by low first-order and high second-order sensitivities.
source: We tested the set of 24 models with synthetic data sets to determine sensitivities, and determined that most parameters showed extensive mutual dependence and compensation, evidenced by the low first-order and high second-order sensitivities (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes sensitivity analysis results.

claim: The top third of models were able to accurately capture the effects of loss of Snail sites from a 700 bp native rho element and correctly characterize modified enhancers with novel Snail sites.
source: Our perturbation dataset did not involve moving Snail binding sites around, however, the top third of models in our test set were able to accurately capture the effects of loss of Snail sites from a 700 bp native rho element, as well as correctly characterize modified enhancers in which novel Snail sites were inserted into active as well as inactive locations (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the predictive performance of models on constructs testing short-range repression.

claim: Heterologous elements from D. melanogaster and homologous rho enhancers from other Drosophila species were successfully modeled by the models trained on the rho dataset.
source: To determine whether modeling from rho can be broadly extended to other regulatory elements, we measured the quantitative output of other enhancers targeted by Dorsal and Twist, and compared their expression patterns with the predictions of a spectrum of our models. Heterologous elements from D. melanogaster and homologous rho enhancers from other Drosophila species were successfully modeled by the models trained on the rho dataset (Figure 5D and Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript describes testing models on independent enhancer sequences.

claim: Analysis of the neuroectodermal brk and sog genes showed that most intergenic sequences did not give rise to any appreciable predicted expression.
source: Analysis of the neuroectodermal brk and sog genes, as well as the more widely expressed twi gene showed that most intergenic sequences did not give rise to any appreciable predicted expression (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes genome scanning results.

claim: A strong consensus among the 24 models for activity was found in two regions flanking the brk gene, which include mapped embryonic enhancers known to bind Dorsal and Twist in vivo.
source: A strong consensus among the 24 models for activity was found in two regions flanking the brk gene; these regions include mapped embryonic enhancers (primary and shadow) that are known to bind Dorsal and Twist in vivo (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript compares model predictions with known enhancer locations.

claim: There were fewer predicted active elements in the region surrounding even-skipped (eve) locus, which is expressed in an anterior-posterior pattern independent of Dorsal/Twist.
source: In contrast, there were fewer predicted active elements in the region surrounding even-skipped (eve) locus, which is expressed in an anterior-posterior pattern independent of Dorsal/Twist.
evidence: The manuscript uses eve as a negative control for model predictions.

claim: The use of multiple models as a predictive 'jury' may help overcome the overfitting that is inherent in modeling.
source: The use of multiple models as a predictive 'jury' may help overcome the overfitting that is inherent in modeling, as the effects of such bias for a given model may be more or less prominent in different contexts.
evidence: This is presented as an interpretation of the ensemble modeling approach.

claim: The arrangement and quality of transcription factor binding sites contains an essential common 'grammar' of cis-regulatory regions that is shared across distinct regulatory elements.
source: Our study indicates that the arrangement and quality of transcription factor binding sites contains an essential common 'grammar' of cis-regulatory regions that is shared across distinct regulatory elements; this stands in contrast to recent studies suggesting that in some cases transcription factors may recognize their target sequences primarily through protein-protein rather than protein-DNA interactions (Kulkarni and Arnosti, 2005; Junion et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful cross-enhancer predictions.

claim: Two features were important for the successful implementation of thermodynamic modeling: development of a high quality perturbation dataset and exploration of a variety of model structures.
source: Two features were important for the successful implementation of this thermodynamic modeling: development of a high quality perturbation dataset, which in our case involved several dozen carefully designed constructs whose transcriptional output was measured quantitatively, and exploration of a variety of model structures.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: Using a panel of models provides a more robust platform for interpreting possible regulatory information than using a single model.
source: As we determined when applying these models to genome discovery, using a panel of models provides a more robust platform for interpreting possible regulatory information; the particular parameter sets developed from fitting the rho perturbation data may represent a certain level of overfitting with respect to all potential Dorsal/Twist target enhancers.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genome scanning results.

claim: For Dorsal and Twist, the modeling predicts strong distance-independent homo- and heterotypic cooperativity between activators, but weak cooperativity between the Snail short-range repressors.
source: Specifically, for Dorsal and Twist, key regulators of dorsal-ventral polarity in the early embryo, our modeling predicts strong distance-independent homo- and heterotypic cooperativity between activators, but weak cooperativity between the Snail short-range repressors.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding from the parameter analysis.

claim: These predicted properties of transcription factor activity are likely linked to chromatin-based activities of these proteins.
source: These effects are likely linked to chromatin-based activities of these proteins (Li and Arnosti, 2011).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The modeling approach was focused on three main regulators of rho activity and did not take into account additional factors such as intrinsic chromatin occupancy, modification of transcription factor activity by signaling, or additional proteins involved in regulation.
source: Our modeling approach was focused on three main regulators of rho activity, and did not take into account additional factors affecting cis-regulatory elements, such as intrinsic chromatin occupancy, modification of transcription factor activity by signaling, or additional proteins involved in regulation of some of the enhancers.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current study.

claim: The study deliberately focused on the early Dorsal regulon for the richness of quantitative resources available to it.
source: Our study has addressed only a fraction of the diversity of factors present in the fly embryo; we deliberately focused on the early Dorsal regulon for the richness of quantitative resources available to it, including transcription factor concentrations, binding specificity of trans-acting factors, and genomic data on in vivo targets.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the system choice.

claim: rho is first expressed in two lateral stripes in the presumptive neurogenic ectoderm of the Drosophila embryo under cooperative activation by Dorsal and Twist.
source: rho is first expressed in two lateral stripes in the presumptive neurogenic ectoderm of the Drosophila embryo under cooperative activation by Dorsal and Twist (Ip et al., 1992; Hong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation support.

claim: Expression is excluded from the mesoderm (ventral region) by Snail, a short-range repressor that interferes with activators located within ~100 bp of a Snail binding site.
source: Expression is excluded from the mesoderm (ventral region) by Snail, a short-range repressor that interferes with activators located within ~100 bp of a Snail binding site (Gray et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation support.

claim: All 38 enhancers were integrated into the fly genome using a site-specific integration vector.
source: All 38 enhancers were cloned and integrated into the fly genome using a site-specific integration vector (Bischof et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Transcriptional output was measured using fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) and confocal laser scanning microscopy.
source: We measured the transcriptional output using fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) and confocal laser scanning microscopy, and analyzed gene expression data using an image-processing pipeline (Ay et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Snail4 and Twist2 sites overlap, which may impair Snail binding and reduce repression efficiency.
source: Snail4 and Twist2 sites overlap, which may impair Snail binding and reduce repression efficiency.
evidence: This is presented as a possible explanation for the observed weak repression by Snail4.

claim: Models trained on the dataset correctly predict activity of evolutionarily divergent regulatory regions.
source: Models trained on the dataset correctly predict activity of evolutionarily divergent regulatory regions, providing insights into spatial relationships between repressor and activator binding sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a key finding.

claim: The collective predictions of sets of models were effective at novel enhancer identification and characterization.
source: Importantly, the collective predictions of sets of models were effective at novel enhancer identification and characterization.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a key finding.

claim: The study demonstrates how experimental dataset and modeling can be effectively combined to provide quantitative insights into cis-regulatory information on a genome-wide scale.
source: Our study demonstrates how experimental dataset and modeling can be effectively combined to provide quantitative insights into cis-regulatory information on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as the main conclusion.

claim: Thermodynamic models employ tools from statistical physics to model gene activity.
source: Thermodynamic models employ tools from statistical physics to model gene activity, providing a framework for understanding transcription factor interactions with specific DNA sequences to regulate gene expression (Bintu et al., 2005; Ay and Arnosti, 2011; Dresch and Drewell, 2012)
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation support.

claim: Previous efforts at thermodynamic modeling in eukaryotic systems have demonstrated that diverse types of data can be fit, providing at least a qualitative level of prediction.
source: Previous efforts at thermodynamic modeling in eukaryotic systems have demonstrated that diverse types of data can be fit, providing at least a qualitative level of prediction (Zinzen et al., 2006; Segal et al., 2008; He et al., 2010; Drewell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation support.

claim: Earlier modeling studies relied on heterogeneous and low-resolution datasets, inherently limiting modeling effectiveness.
source: However, earlier studies relied on heterogeneous and low-resolution datasets, inherently limiting modeling effectiveness.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work.
